---
title: "Finding phrases with readable rules"
subtitle: "Evaluate a credential pattern before using its results"
description: "Learn how simple string rules find credential phrases, how concordances help inspection, and why rules need maintenance."
categories: [phrases and entities, rule-based matching, workforce research]
---

Credential requirements are easy to miss in a short job-board feed. The
Riverton Workforce Lab starts with a readable rule, then examines whether the rule
answers the same question a reviewer would ask.

Readability does not establish correctness.
A pattern can find real mentions, miss differently worded mentions, or match
the same word with a different meaning.

::: {.callout-note}
The author created the fictional Riverton Workforce Lab, its job board, and
its training flyer for teaching.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## What you will learn

After this lesson, you should be able to:

- write small phrase rules with stringr.
- extract the matched credential word.
- apply a written hand-marking rule for required credentials.
- count false positives and false negatives without treating the counts as a rate.
- use a concordance to examine matches in context.
:::

```{r}
#| include: false

options(warn = 2)
stopifnot(identical(getOption("warn"), 2L))
```

## Write the first rules

The setup chunk reads the Riverton sentences, builds rule-result tables, handles
regular expressions, and prepares a concordance. In stringr, regular expressions
use the ICU engine and its rules for boundaries and letter classes.

```{r}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(tidyr)
library(stringr)
library(quanteda)

sentences <- read_csv(
  "data/workforce/workforce_sentences.csv",
  na = character(),
  col_types = cols(
    sentence_id = col_character(),
    document_id = col_character(),
    source_line = col_character(),
    text = col_character(),
    reference_label = col_character(),
    uncertainty = col_character(),
    annotator_id = col_character(),
    rationale = col_character(),
    codebook_version = col_character(),
    codebook_hash = col_character(),
    derived = col_character(),
    transformation = col_character()
  )
)

credential_terms <- c("certificate", "certification", "licen[cs]e")
credential_pattern <- regex(
  str_c("\\b(", str_c(credential_terms, collapse = "|"), ")\\b"),
  ignore_case = TRUE
)

rule_results <- sentences |>
  mutate(
    rule_match = str_detect(text, credential_pattern),
    matched_word = str_extract(text, credential_pattern),
    hand_required_credential = sentence_id %in% c("s005", "s017")
  )

matched_rows <- rule_results |>
  filter(rule_match | hand_required_credential) |>
  select(sentence_id, text, matched_word, rule_match, hand_required_credential)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  matched_rows,
  col.names = c("Sentence ID", "Text", "Matched word", "Rule matched", "Hand-marked required credential"),
  caption = "Rule matches and hand markings for required credentials",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(all(
  c("readr", "dplyr", "tibble", "tidyr", "stringr", "quanteda") %in%
    loadedNamespaces()
))

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(sentences), 28L),
  identical(sum(rule_results$rule_match), 4L),
  identical(sum(rule_results$hand_required_credential), 2L),
  identical(
    matched_rows$sentence_id,
    c("s005", "s006", "s013", "s017", "s024")
  ),
  identical(
    as.character(na.omit(matched_rows$matched_word)),
    c("certification", "certificate", "license", "CERTIFICATE")
  )
)
```

The rule searches for `certificate`, `certification`, and either spelling of
`license`. The author hand-marked each text unit under this definition:

Mark a unit only when it states an employer requirement for a formal
qualification. The qualification must come from a school, licensing body, or
certifying organisation. Do not mark a unit that merely mentions a
qualification.

Under that rule, `s005` and `s017` qualify.
One reviewer applying one rule to 28 units provides a worked example, not a
reference standard.

## Score the rule

A **false positive** is a text unit that the rule puts a mark on but the hand
marking rejects. A **false negative** is a unit that the hand marking accepts
but the rule misses. The pattern searches for credential words.
The hand marking instead marks required credentials.
The pattern has no requirement condition, so it can match `preferred` or a
heading.

```{r}
score_counts <- rule_results |>
  summarise(
    true_positive = sum(rule_match & hand_required_credential),
    false_positive = sum(rule_match & !hand_required_credential),
    false_negative = sum(!rule_match & hand_required_credential),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "result",
    values_to = "sentences"
  )

false_positive_ids <- rule_results |>
  filter(rule_match & !hand_required_credential) |>
  pull(sentence_id)
false_negative_ids <- rule_results |>
  filter(!rule_match & hand_required_credential) |>
  pull(sentence_id)

problem_examples <- tibble(
  result = c("false positive", "false negative"),
  sentence_id = c("s006", "s005"),
  explanation = c(
    "The line says the employer pays for certification training, not that certification is required.",
    "The line says a diploma is required, but diploma was not in the rule."
  )
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  score_counts,
  col.names = c("Result", "Text units"),
  caption = "Text-unit counts for the first credential rule",
  row.names = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(
  problem_examples,
  col.names = c("Result", "Sentence ID", "Explanation"),
  caption = "One false positive and one false negative",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(score_counts$sentences, c(1L, 3L, 1L)),
  identical(false_positive_ids, c("s006", "s013", "s024")),
  identical(false_negative_ids, "s005"),
  problem_examples$sentence_id[problem_examples$result == "false positive"] %in% false_positive_ids,
  problem_examples$sentence_id[problem_examples$result == "false negative"] %in% false_negative_ids,
  identical(rule_results$matched_word[rule_results$sentence_id == "s017"], "license")
)
```

For required credentials, 3 of the 4 matches are wrong.
The rule also misses 1 of the 2 hand-marked positives.
Two positives cannot establish general performance.
These counts illustrate failures. Both `certificate` and `certification` can
appear without a requirement, while the pattern omits `diploma`.

## Examine matches in context

A **concordance** lists every occurrence of a word in text.
The usual display is **keyword in context**, or **KWIC**.
It places the matched word between a few words of preceding and following
context.

```{r}
riverton_corpus <- corpus(setNames(sentences$text, sentences$sentence_id))
riverton_tokens <- tokens(riverton_corpus, remove_punct = TRUE)

credential_kwic <- kwic(
  riverton_tokens,
  pattern = credential_terms,
  window = 4,
  valuetype = "regex",
  case_insensitive = TRUE
) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  as_tibble() |>
  select(docname, pre, keyword, post)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  credential_kwic,
  col.names = c("Sentence ID", "Before", "Keyword", "After"),
  caption = "Concordance lines for the credential rule",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(credential_kwic), 4L),
  identical(credential_kwic$docname, c("s006", "s013", "s017", "s024")),
  identical(str_to_lower(credential_kwic$keyword), c("certification", "certificate", "license", "certificate")),
  identical(credential_kwic$post[credential_kwic$docname == "s006"], "training")
)
```

The KWIC display shows why the pattern needs revision.
Its token-level regex uses the same credential terms as the scoring pattern.
It finds `certification training`, a preferred `certificate`, a required
`license`, and a flyer heading.

## What to remember

- A readable rule can still answer the wrong question.
- This first credential rule has 1 true positive, 3 false positives, and 1 false negative.
- Two hand-marked positives are enough for a worked example, not for a performance estimate.
- KWIC lines show reviewers why a pattern matched.

Use this pattern only to select text for further checks.
In the next revision, evaluate requirement language before adding credential
terms.
